So-called dollar price guide

Estimated values for slabbed so-called dollars by Hibler-Kappen number and grade: 295 pieces with sales of their own, and 972 more, shown in blue, that have no sales in the records we gathered and are estimated from the formula alone. Edition of November 2026. How we make these figures.

Our opinion, not a promise

These are Tokens and Medals' own estimates from a statistical formula. They are not appraisals, not offers to buy or sell, and not a prediction of what your piece will bring. Real prices at any venue can land well above or below them; about one sale in five lands outside the range shown. Do not rely on this guide alone to buy, sell, insure or value a piece for tax or estate purposes.

Figures in blue, marked “formula only”, are extrapolations. We have no sales of those pieces in the records we gathered, so there is no price data for the piece itself: the figure comes only from what similar pieces bring, and it is much less certain.

How to read it

  • The bold figure is our estimate for the piece in that grade as it would sell today at a major numismatic auction. The smaller figures are the range we expect about four sales in five to land in.
  • PCGS and NGC holders are priced separately: in the sales we studied, NGC-slabbed pieces brought about 23% less than the same piece and grade in a PCGS holder.
  • Weekly online auctions ran about 20% below the major floor auctions, and eBay about 20% below. Take that much off the figures for those venues.
  • A piece with sales lists the grades it exists in, within three points of a grade it has sold in; further from the evidence we would rather say nothing. A formula-only piece lists up to six of the grades it is most often found in.
  • Blue figures are formula-only estimates for pieces with no sales in our records. We tested the same method on 201 sales that were the first of their piece in our records, each predicted before that sale: half came within 44% of the figure, and 79% fell inside the range, which is much wider than for pieces with sales. Use the switch above the list to hide them.
  • Prices include the metal. Where we have a piece’s weight and fineness from two kinds of source (1 piece so far), its figures never go below the metal, and its heading says so. For the other gold and silver pieces, check the melt value too; if the metal is worth more than our figure, the metal wins.

Gold $4,070.58 · silver $51.95 an ounce: the Chainlink price on 2026-11-07, when this edition was built. With JavaScript on, the page updates the pieces with confirmed metal content to the live price.

How we make these figures

The formula was built from public auction results of the major numismatic auction houses and from completed eBay sales of slabbed pieces. We studied those sales; none of them is reproduced here.

What goes in

  • Grade. Each grade point is worth about 10%.
  • Metal. Silver pieces bring about 1.9 times what the same kind of piece brings in copper or bronze, and gold about 3.3 times. The metal comes from the Hibler-Kappen catalogue or the grading service's own label, never from a guess.
  • Scarcity. How often the piece turned up for sale between 1970 and 2000. A piece seen twice as often brings about 22% less.
  • Age. When it was issued. Older issues bring more.
  • The holder (PCGS or NGC), the venue and the season. The holder is included because PCGS and NGC pieces plainly sell differently, even though it added little to the test scores; the venue and the season earned their place in the tests. Spring and summer sales ran about 16% below January-to-March ones; the guide averages over the year.
  • The date of the sale. Prices have drifted up about 3% a year. Every estimate is brought forward to today.
  • The piece's own sales. Each past sale is adjusted to today's grade, holder and venue, recent sales count for more, and the result is blended with what similar pieces bring, so one odd result can't set the price on its own.

Pieces with no sales in our records

For a piece with no sales in our records, the figure is the formula's value from its metal, grade, age, how often it turned up for sale between 1970 and 2000, and what other pieces from the same event bring, with no adjustment from sales of its own. To see whether that can be trusted, we went back through every sale since 2016 that was the first sale of its piece in our records, and predicted it using only the sales before it: 201 such sales in all. Half landed within 44% of the figure, and the range shown caught 79% of them when tested on pieces it had not been set from. We also checked whether rare pieces, or pieces from events with no sales at all, needed their own ranges; they did not hold up better, so one range is used. Gold pieces with no sales in our records are left out: there were too few first gold sales in our records to test against.

What we tested and left out

Copper colour designations (BN, RB, RD), CAC stickers, plus grades, how many pieces have been slabbed, the number struck and diameter were all tried. None of them improved the predictions of sales the formula hadn't seen reliably enough to keep, so none is used. The guide does not price colour designations separately.

How well it works

We predicted every sale from 2016 on using only the sales that came before it. Half of those sales landed within 29% of our figure. For scale, even a perfect estimate would miss a typical single sale by about 22%: that is how much sales of the same piece in the same grade scatter around their typical price. The range caught 79% of the sales in that test, and 76% of the sales since 2024.

What isn't listed

Gold pieces with no sales in our records, pieces whose metal is not stated by the catalogue or the grading service, restrikes, and grades below AU55. Pieces with no sales in our records are also left out when the PCGS and NGC population reports we read show no slab of them at AU55 or above (some, such as HK-3, appear there only in a Details holder), or when their slab labels give no year. A piece missing from the guide is not a sign that it is common or rare.
